teacher_review_theme: Atomizer pressure mechanism versus full application analysis
scientific_teacher_note: Lower pressure at the perfume pickup opening relative to the liquid surface drives perfume upward, original A. It is a valid practical scenario but teacher source marks Understanding; verify whether the inference reaches official B44 Application-level analysis or keep as supportive practice.

teacher_review_theme: Distinguish aspiration from atomization
scientific_teacher_note: Faster airflow can strengthen liquid entrainment and breakup into finer droplets, original C. The Bernoulli pressure difference helps lift liquid; aerodynamic shear and liquid properties also affect drop size, so avoid claiming Bernoulli pressure alone determines droplet size.

teacher_review_theme: Filter pump recognition versus application
scientific_teacher_note: The original NBF printed p101–102 depicts a filter pump using running water to draw air from a connected vessel, so A is the best device. Merely selecting the device name is a recall/recognition question and not itself the B44 Summative/Application analysis expected for a certified final exam.

teacher_review_theme: Blocked side port disrupts suction
scientific_teacher_note: Closing the suction side tube prevents the jet's low-pressure region from drawing air out of the vessel, so original A is supported. The answer describes immediate air removal rather than all possible transient pressure effects in the connected apparatus.

teacher_review_theme: Deeper orifice means greater head
scientific_teacher_note: With equal free-surface reference, open reservoir and negligible losses, v=sqrt(2gh) gives greater initial exit speed from deeper hole, original A. The word initially is appropriate because a draining tank's head evolves with time.

teacher_review_theme: Outlet speed scales as square root of head
scientific_teacher_note: For the same ideal model, h→2h gives v2/v1=√2, original D, not double speed or quadruple. The stem explicitly fixes surface elevation and simplifies outlet conditions.

teacher_review_theme: Denser fluid comparison is theoretical
scientific_teacher_note: The ideal open-tank equal ambient-pressure derivation cancels rho in rho gh=½rho v²; at identical h and g the predicted v is unchanged, original A. This compares separate ideal liquids; changes in real viscosity, surface tension and exit coefficients can alter measured efflux.

teacher_review_theme: Draining tank treated as sequence of steady states
scientific_teacher_note: As h decreases gradually, ideal v=sqrt(2gh) decreases (B). A draining tank is time-varying overall, so apply Torricelli instantaneously under quasi-steady large-tank assumptions rather than pretending h remains constant.

teacher_review_theme: Constricted ideal pipe speed and pressure
scientific_teacher_note: For steady incompressible unbranched fixed-Q flow a narrower section has higher mean speed, while same-height ideal no-loss Bernoulli predicts lower static pressure; source D. The question combines continuity B36 with the B40/B44 pressure concept and explicitly calls the flow ideal.

teacher_review_theme: Piezometer reading depends on common fluid/datum; U versus A
scientific_teacher_note: Taller hydrostatic column above the wider section supports higher local static pressure there, source A, provided the taps reference the same elevation and same piezometer fluid open to the same atmosphere. The source author tags Understanding; justify whether the figure/data inference qualifies as B44 Application before exam certification.

teacher_review_theme: Fixed pressure difference and area ratio with changed density
scientific_teacher_note: In an ideal fixed-geometry Venturi at a constant measured ΔP, v∝1/sqrt(rho), so smaller rho gives greater inferred speed, source A. This compares separate ideal fluids/conditions, not a single incompressible stream changing its density spontaneously.

teacher_review_theme: High-speed carburetor throat draws fuel
scientific_teacher_note: Original NBF printed p104 shows a fast narrow air passage with lower local static pressure that favours fuel aspiration, source D. Actual fuel metering includes jets and engineering details; interpretation remains idealized.

teacher_review_theme: Backward-labelled Venturi still obeys continuity
scientific_teacher_note: In steady incompressible throughflow without branches, v=Q/A, so the smaller section has greater mean speed even if meter labels are reversed (C). This is directly official B36 continuity Application, not on its own applying B40 pressure-speed-height Bernoulli; the prepared author's B40 tag is provisional.

teacher_review_theme: Aircraft wing pressure difference times area
scientific_teacher_note: (100−97)kPa×12m²=3000Pa×12m²=36000N upward, source A. This assumes the quoted upper/lower pressures describe the representative pressure difference across an effective area; real aerodynamic lift involves distributed pressure and shear.

teacher_review_theme: Equal transit time is not a law
scientific_teacher_note: Source A correctly rejects the erroneous equal-arrival-time claim. The original simplified aerofoil figure depicts differing paths, but equal transit time is not necessary to explain lift. Teacher must explicitly prevent the longer-path-equal-time misconception and approve suitability as B44 Application analysis.

teacher_review_theme: Reverse spin changes transverse force direction
scientific_teacher_note: Reversing spin can change the direction of pressure/flow asymmetry around a moving cricket ball and alter lateral Magnus deflection, source B. This conditional real-world reasoning is correct; teacher's Understanding tag must be individually reviewed against B44 Summative/Application demand.

teacher_review_theme: Opposite spin can reverse Magnus-force sign
scientific_teacher_note: At similar velocity and environmental conditions, reversed spin can produce opposite sideways Magnus forces, source C. The word may is scientifically justified. Source teacher Understanding does not by itself prove official B44 Application-level classification.

teacher_review_theme: Two-sheet activity tests formative Bernoulli effect
scientific_teacher_note: Original printed NBF p101 shows two sheets pulled inward when air flows rapidly between them; lower pressure between sheets (D) is correct in idealized class demonstration. This is chiefly formative P-11-B-39 qualitative effect, not automatically summative B44 real-world device analysis; keep as study practice pending SLO review.

teacher_review_theme: Lower height and smaller speed both raise static pressure
scientific_teacher_note: For an ideal constant-density streamline between a higher and a lower point, lower h and lower v both reduce other Bernoulli terms so local P can be higher (C). A pipe can slow while descending if its flow area expands; no numeric pressure is asserted.

teacher_review_theme: Assignment 6.4 simplified airfoil model, compressibility and common head
scientific_teacher_note: Original NBF printed p106 Assignment6.4 specifies airflow speeds 450 and 410m/s and uses a simplified wing-lift calculation. Source D is the best offered answer because it acknowledges a simplified Bernoulli model and comparable heights, but those speeds exceed ordinary sound speed: real aircraft flow is compressible and may include shocks. Comparing top/bottom local speeds from different streamlines requires equivalent upstream total head, pressure/flow model and loss assumptions. This item must not be treated as validating real wing lift from speeds alone without explicit teacher caveat.
